entry.evidence: This snow cover product provides an opportunity for a rapid and quantitative examination of seasonal variability, altitude-wise variability, and temporal trends

steps.action: Reviewed published reports of regional warming and of snow and glacier decline over the HKH that vary by season, longitude and altitude.
steps.quote: Recent studies indicate that the trend of snow cover also shows large variations with altitude.

steps.action: Took the MODIS MOD10 snow product and its field-based accuracy assessments, including its known overestimation in the Everest region, from other groups' work.
steps.quote: have evaluated the performance of these snow products based on field measurements

steps.action: Posed the aim of building hypsographic curves of seasonal distribution and temporal trend of snow cover with altitude, together with a zonal analysis.
steps.quote: one of the primary objectives of this current study is to create hypsographic curves

steps.action: Obtained MOD10CM v6 monthly 5 km snow cover for March 2000 to February 2017, masked fill codes, clipped it to the ICIMOD HKH boundary, and paired it with SRTM 90 m DEM elevations resampled to 5 km.
steps.quote: Monthly average snow cover in 5 km resolution (collection 6; product MOD10CM) was obtained

steps.action: Designed the analysis: five 10° longitudinal zones, melting (Mar-Aug) and accumulating (Sep-Feb) seasons, hypsographic aggregation, and per-pixel LIN trends with Theil-Sen and Mann-Kendall statistics for significance.
steps.quote: The HKH region was further divided into five different longitudinal zones (west to east)

steps.action: Mapped long-term mean snow cover, its persistence over 204 months and permanent (>80 %) snow, and tabulated means by month, altitude band and zone.
steps.quote: The average long-term snow cover is found to be 35.9 % (Table 1)

steps.action: Established the repeating seasonal cycle (rise Sep-Feb, fall Mar-Aug) and the year-to-year hypsographic structure, with a sharp jump between about 5000 and 6400 m and low variability above 6400 m.
steps.quote: there is an overall gradual increase in the mean snow cover from September to February

steps.action: Attributed the anomalous low-altitude (<1000 m, <800 m) snow cover and its variability to topographic shadows in the retrieval algorithm, and the low 2016 value to missing January-February data, rather than to real snow.
steps.quote: This increase in interannual variability at lower altitudes may be attributed to known issues such as topographic shadows in the snow cover retrieval algorithm.

steps.action: Built seasonal and monthly hypsographic curves showing accumulating > melting season between 800 and 5400 m, and a roughly 1-month lag at 5500-7000 m, and explained the lag by thin seasonal snow at lower altitudes.
steps.quote: The higher-altitude snow cover (5500–7000 m) shows a lag (approx. 1 month) in the starting of the melting and accumulation phases.

steps.action: Fitted a linear trend to the regional monthly mean time series and found a very weak, statistically insignificant decline over the whole HKH.
steps.quote: shows a very weak and statistically insignificant negative trend (or decline) of snow cover over the entire study area

steps.action: Set the insignificant regional trend against prior ground and satellite studies and argued that regional and altitudinal analyses are needed.
steps.quote: [...] to several studies and databases, based on ground and satellite observations, over the last 2–3 decades

steps.action: Computed per-pixel linear trends at 5 km and mapped the statistically significant (95 % CI) increases in the central Himalaya and northern Nepal and the decreases in Arunachal Pradesh, the eastern Himalaya and Tibet.
steps.quote: shows large spatial variability, as calculated from the slope of the linear fit

steps.action: Compared the eastern decline with published image and glacier-area studies (Prasad and Singh 2007; Basnett et al. 2013) and found them consistent.
steps.quote: Snow and glacier images from Arunachal Pradesh show a large decline in snow cover and signs of glacier melting

steps.action: Aggregated the trends by altitude (100 m and 1 m bins), for the whole region and for significant pixels only, and found losses of about -5 % at 4001-4500 and 5501-6000 m.
steps.quote: clearly indicates an overall loss in snow cover with altitude

steps.action: Recomputed the altitude-wise trend with Theil-Sen median slopes and Mann-Kendall z scores and found peaks at the same altitudes as the LIN fit.
steps.quote: We obtained a similar linear trend from median trend analysis (TS) and the monotonic trend (MK statistics).

steps.action: Broke the LIN trends down by zone and 500 m band, with the strongest decline in Zone 5 (about -11.2 % at 4501-5000 m) and increases above 6000 m in Zones 2-4.
steps.quote: this decline varies widely for different altitudes and zones (west to east)

steps.action: Extrapolated the altitude-band linear trends to estimate the time for a roughly 25 % decline in mean snow cover.
steps.quote: it may take 76–94 years for approximately 25 % decline in the mean snow cover

steps.action: Kept the zonal and altitudinal trend estimates as preliminary findings and called for longer records and continued monitoring.
steps.quote: a substantial decline in some specific zones/regions that were observed from a temporal trend analysis is a cause for concern

tree.answer: Spatial, seasonal and altitudinal variability and trend of HKH snow cover, 2000-2017
Partly: snow fraction is retrieved from MODIS NDSI; trends are inferred by fitting
Describe hypsographic and zonal distribution and estimate trends
Conditions found, from an existing satellite archive
Altitude-wise trend agrees across LIN, Theil-Sen and Mann-Kendall

end.claim: At 5 km and 100 m altitude bins, snow cover over the HKH declined most (about 5 % or more in significant regions) at 4000-4500 and 5500-6000 m during 2000-2017, while the region-wide trend was weak and insignificant, with large zonal contrasts (decline in the east, increases in the west and above 6000 m).

decisive_move.sentence: Aggregating the per-pixel linear trends by altitude (hypsographic trend curves for all and for significant pixels) produced the headline altitude bands of decline; without it there is no claim.

gates.evidence: The data are an existing MODIS archive collected without a hypothesis (§2.3 ¶1). Pixel trends were tested for significance at 95 % CI, and the altitude-wise trend was cross-checked with TS and MK, which could have disagreed (§3.3 ¶2, §3.3 ¶4); no rival hypothesis was tested. Zones, seasons and methods are not reported as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Theil-Sen median trend (robust exploratory data analysis, Hoaglin et al. 2000)

limits: No review file or open discussion was supplied, although the paper went through public discussion (started 3 June 2021) and three referees, so no review sequence is coded. Trend estimates carry no stated uncertainty beyond 95 % significance masks, so 'estimate_with_resolution' rests on 5 km and 100 m resolution and significance only. The paper does not validate MOD10CM in the HKH itself: accuracy is cited (step 2), and low-altitude artifacts are attributed to topographic shadows without correction (step 8, a protective move). Internal inconsistencies: the abstract gives ~74 to 7900 years for a 25 % decline, while §3.3 ¶6 and §4 give 76-94 years and 'hundreds or thousands'; the text refers to a 'Figure 6c' but Figure 6 has only panels a-b; §3.1 ¶2 labels '(100–105 ∘ E)' as Zone 4. Inference: it is not stated whether the seasonal cycle was removed before fitting per-pixel trends on monthly series, or whether significance maps were corrected for multiple testing. The 2016 data gap enters Table 2 and Figure 3. Sub-claims: the seasonal cycle and hypsographic snow-cover structure (regularity_in_range, from 17 repeated years); zonal and altitudinal trend breakdowns (estimate_with_resolution); time-to-25 %-decline extrapolations (estimate, weak, linear extrapolation far beyond the 17-year record). Consistency with Prasad and Singh (2007) and Basnett et al. (2013) is a qualitative comparison with cited independent data, coded as replication not performed here. Composition is none_fits: a descriptive estimation from an existing archive with no rivals and no exploration-until-stable or capability-first structure; natures_repetition is the closest, but the claim is a trend estimate, not a fitted regularity. The V coding is full, from one method check; there is no triangulation.

disagreements.target: Several studies and databases ( [...] ., 2007; Bolch, 2007; Kulkarni, 2006; Raup et al., 2007) showing snow cover changes [...]
disagreements.support: The region-wide MODIS trend for 2000-2016 is weak and insignificant, which the authors take to mean that change is regional and altitudinal rather than uniform.
disagreements.quote: [...] to several studies and databases, based on ground and satellite observations, over the last 2–3 decades

alternatives_considered.chosen: Linear trend (LIN, Pearson), reported alongside Theil-Sen median trend and Mann-Kendall significance
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Median trend analysis (TS) and Mann-Kendall monotonic trend (MK)
alternatives_considered.reason: LIN is sensitive to noise in shorter series; TS is reliable for short or noisy series; MK assesses significance

alternatives_considered.chosen: Altitude-wise trend shown both for statistically significant pixels and for the entire region
